title: A Conversation with Sabastian Niles on the Legal Profession in the Agentic AI Era
pub: Harvard Law School Center on the Legal Profession — Insights (clp.law.harvard.edu)
author: Sabastian Niles · David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The excerpt provides only personal and intellectual context for Niles’s agentic-AI letter. It offers no specific claim or evidence about legal-workforce restructuring, broad displacement, or heightened risks to junior pipelines, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Niles accepts the shift toward multistep, workflow-wide delegation while materially developing the cluster’s governance account: agents should have defined roles, access, prohibitions and enforceable controls, with strong human oversight for legal work. His claimed workflow benefits remain largely executive assertions rather than quantified evidence, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: Just as importantly: what is it explicitly not allowed to do—and how do we enforce that?
But especially in legal, where risk, accountability, and trust are central, we maintain strong human oversight—and ultimately augment and support that oversight with cutting-edge technology.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Niles accepts AI as an operating-model transformation and materially develops the cluster’s bargaining thesis from the buyer side: legal departments should unbundle work, allocate it deliberately among internal teams, firms, other providers and tools, and require digitally mature, governed collaboration. His Salesforce examples add an implementation model, though benefits are reported rather than quantitatively established.
qs: I think we’re moving toward a new shared operating system for risk, judgment, and execution—across companies, law firms, and other advisors.
How do we break work into components and match each piece to the right provider or tool?

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Niles accepts that AI value depends on organisational and workflow redesign, then extends the proposition with a cross-organisational operating model linking clients, law firms and advisors. He adds concrete governance requirements—trust, accountability, auditability and explainability—while treating changes in purchasing and pricing as questions rather than established outcomes.
qs: I think we’re moving toward a new shared operating system for risk, judgment, and execution—across companies, law firms, and other advisors.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Niles accepts the cluster’s human-led, selectively deployed model and materially extends it with a concrete enterprise operating approach: governed agents with explicit permissions and oversight, cross-platform human–AI teaming, and decomposition of legal work across internal teams, firms and tools. His Salesforce examples support feasibility, although they do not provide quantitative evidence of realised value.
qs: But especially in legal, where risk, accountability, and trust are central, we maintain strong human oversight—and ultimately augment and support that oversight with cutting-edge technology.
How do we break work into components and match each piece to the right provider or tool?

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: Niles accepts the cluster’s workflow-based account of trust and materially extends it to firm–client collaboration. He specifies visibility, observability, auditability and explainability as governance requirements for regulated, cross-organisational workflows, while treating trust as something shaped by how advisers deploy AI rather than by AI reliability alone. He does not, however, provide evidence on verification costs.
qs: That’s also how you defend regulated workflows—and it should also apply to how law firms and clients work together.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Niles supports the cluster’s core view that value depends on organisational absorption rather than tool procurement alone. He emphasises cross-functional workflow redesign, investment in human AI capabilities, retained human oversight and explicit agent permissions and guardrails, while presenting Salesforce’s agentic legal function as an ambition rather than measured evidence of realised buyer gains.
qs: How do we build integrated, cross‑functional, cross‑silo workflows where humans and agents collaborate effectively?
Just as importantly: what is it explicitly not allowed to do—and how do we enforce that?

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Niles supports redesigning legal delivery around client value, shared firm–client workflows and governed human–AI collaboration. His emphasis on auditability, permissions and human review aligns with the cluster’s verification and implementation constraints, though he offers a leadership vision rather than evidence on pricing, staffing or apprenticeship effects.
qs: I think we’re moving toward a new shared operating system for risk, judgment, and execution—across companies, law firms, and other advisors.

kp.k: Internal agents support legal self-service and higher-stakes human work
kp.d: In this July 2026 interview, Niles describes Salesforce's legal, compliance and risk teams using Slackbot internally, with the legal team training it to answer internal clients' questions and propose plans. He asserts that this frees lawyers to focus on trust and high-stakes complexity; the interview provides operational descriptions rather than measured productivity results.
qs: Slackbot – which brings together context, conversation, and action directly in the flow of work – is trained by our legal team to respond to internal clients.
This includes answering questions, proposing plans, and doing it at scale with our legal judgment baked in.
Tools like Slackbot free up our legal team to focus on continuing to build trust and navigate high-stakes complexity.

kp.k: Clients expect digital maturity and collaborative innovation from firms
kp.d: Niles says Salesforce expects external firms and other partners to meet its own digital-maturity standards. He describes real-time collaboration through Slack Connect and LCAio, a joint legal innovation and legal operations group that co-develops solutions with outside firms and service providers.
qs: We also expect our vendors and trusted partners—including law firms—to show the same level of digital maturity we hold ourselves to.

We also created LCAio, a joint innovation group that combines our legal innovation and legal ops teams under one roof and partners with outside law firms and innovative service providers to co‑develop solutions.

kp.k: In-house lawyers become purchasers and capital stewards
kp.d: Niles frames the in-house role as extending beyond judgment and execution to deliberate allocation of finite company resources. An outside counsel support agent handles common questions, workflows and recurring tasks, while the broader recommendation is to decompose matters and select internal lawyers, external firms, other providers or tools for individual components.
qs: An example is our “outside counsel support agent.” It helps firms and our internal teams manage common issues—questions, workflows, recurring tasks.
We’re not just providers of judgment and execution; we’re also sophisticated purchasers and stewards of the company’s capital.
Which matters should the internal team handle? Which should go to external firms? How do we break work into components and match each piece to the right provider or tool?

kp.k: Workflow-wide agent deployment retains strong human oversight
kp.d: Niles characterizes embedding agents throughout workflows as both Salesforce's goal and current reality, identifying intake, triage and routing while placing assignment and execution further along the trajectory. He claims faster responses and self-service reduce friction and risk and accelerate business priorities, but emphasizes strong human oversight in legal work. These are company-reported benefits and ambitions, without quantified outcomes.
qs: Our goal—and our reality now—is to embed AI agents into every workflow.
They help with intake, triage, routing, and eventually assignment and execution.

When response time accelerates, when internal clients are empowered through effective self-serve delivery models and when our global teams are augmented with agentic capabilities, we remove friction, mitigate risk, simplify processes and advance business priorities faster.
But especially in legal, where risk, accountability, and trust are central, we maintain strong human oversight—and ultimately augment and support that oversight with cutting-edge technology.

kp.k: Autonomous processes require deliberate architecture and governance
kp.d: Niles describes movement toward agents that reason, plan and act for individuals, teams and the company. He presents choices between probabilistic and deterministic processes, supporting infrastructure, controls and governance as essential design questions, drawing an explicit analogy to legal debates about rules versus standards rather than reporting a settled technical solution.
qs: We’re moving toward autonomous processes and agents that can responsibly reason, plan, and act on behalf of individuals, teams, and the company.

What should be probabilistic, what should be deterministic and what are the building blocks for the agentic harness that provides the critical scaffolding, context and operating system to convert raw model intelligence into trusted transformation?
Where do we set guardrails, deploy controls and implement effective governance and trust?
To me, that echoes classic legal debates about rules versus standards.

kp.k: AI prompts reconsideration of what clients purchase
kp.d: Niles asks whether clients buy hours, documents, judgment, risk management, speed or outcomes, and anticipates a shared operating system for risk, judgment and execution across companies and advisors. This is a prospective reframing of legal-service value, not evidence that hourly billing has been replaced or a specific recommendation for a fee arrangement.
qs: From the client’s perspective, this moment forces us to ask a very basic set of questions: What are we buying, why are we partnering, and who should we trust?

When we engage law firms and other professional service and advisory forms, are we buying inputs (time, hours)? Outputs (documents, memos)? Judgment? Risk mitigation, allocation and transfer? Speed? Outcomes?
I think we’re moving toward a new shared operating system for risk, judgment, and execution—across companies, law firms, and other advisors.

kp.k: Client AI restrictions raise trust and accountability questions
kp.d: Niles reports that some clients prohibit AI use and that firms can cite these restrictions as barriers to innovation. He asks whether this reflects innovation avoidance or concerns about how AI is used, without resolving the question empirically. He recommends enterprise-style visibility, observability, auditability and explainability for regulated workflows and firm-client relationships.
qs: You need visibility, observability, auditability and explainability.
That’s also how you defend regulated workflows—and it should also apply to how law firms and clients work together.
Some clients have told their law firms, “You shall not use AI.”

Is this really about innovation avoidance—using client concerns and mandates as an excuse? Or is it fundamentally about trust and understanding? Do clients distrust AI, or do they distrust how AI might be used?

kp.k: Trusted agents need defined roles, permissions and enforceable limits
kp.d: Niles recommends human-aligned, reliable systems whose roles, data access, operating channels, permitted tasks and prohibitions are specified and enforced. His analogy is organizational governance of employees: agents need comparable clarity about responsibilities and behavioral constraints.
qs: My view is that we need to move into what I call “trusted agentics”: intelligent systems that are human‑aligned, reliable, and deserving of trust.
What is the agent’s role? What data can it access? In what channels does it operate (Slack, phone, email, other tools)? What tasks is it allowed to perform?
Just as importantly: what is it explicitly not allowed to do—and how do we enforce that?
Employees have roles, responsibilities, permissions, and codes of conduct. AI agents need the same clarity.

kp.k: Human-agent teaming demands investment in AI fluency
kp.d: Niles identifies cross-platform human-AI teamwork and integrated workflows across functions and silos as the next challenge for both legal departments and law firms. He calls for investment in people's agentic capabilities and AI fluency, drawing on ideas from frontline staff as well as leadership.
qs: The real frontier is teaming: not just human‑human teams, but human‑AI teams across platforms.
How do we build integrated, cross‑functional, cross‑silo workflows where humans and agents collaborate effectively?

How and where do we invest in our people to build their agentic capabilities, elevate their level of AI fluency, help them do the best work of their careers and empower our teams to leverage these cutting-edge technologies in the ways that our people on the front line as well as those in leadership positions know will have the most impact?
That’s the challenge ahead for in‑house departments and law firms alike.

kp.k: Senior expertise complements curiosity and AI delegation
kp.d: Wilkins frames AI supervision as analogous to senior lawyers' existing delegation practices: providing context, reviewing and interrogating returned work, and applying expertise. Niles agrees and advocates combining a beginner's mind with accumulated legal knowledge, pattern recognition, judgment and professional norms rather than discarding that expertise.
qs: They already know how to delegate work: they give context, review what comes back, interrogate it, then add their own deep, domain‑specific expertise.
A phrase I often use with law firm partners, internal teams, and business leaders is “the beginner’s mind blended with expertise.”
We don’t throw out the accumulated body of legal work. We respect it, extend it, and apply it in new ways.
Senior lawyers bring decades of pattern recognition, judgment, and professional norms.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Niles says Salesforce already uses AI to deliver internal legal assistance at scale, freeing lawyers to focus on trust and high-stakes complexity.
pts.d: Niles describes Slackbot as trained by Salesforce's legal team to answer internal clients' questions and propose plans with the team's legal judgment embedded. He also describes an outside counsel support agent that assists internal teams and firms with questions, workflows and recurring tasks. These are reported deployments and qualitative benefit claims, rather than predictions of wholesale lawyer replacement.

pts.k: Niles claims embedded agents and self-service legal delivery accelerate work and compound operational benefits, with greater autonomous execution ahead.
pts.d: Niles characterizes embedding agents into workflows as both a current reality and a goal. He identifies intake, triage and routing as functions agents support, while describing assignment and execution as eventual extensions. He claims faster responses, self-service and augmented teams reduce friction and risk and advance business priorities. His projected autonomy remains qualified by responsible operation and strong human oversight, particularly in legal.

pts.k: Niles predicts a more integrated operating relationship between clients, law firms and advisors, alongside more deliberate allocation of work among teams, providers and tools.
pts.d: Niles presents in-house lawyers as purchasers and capital stewards as well as providers of judgment and execution. He calls for disaggregating work and matching components to appropriate resources, and predicts a shared operating system for risk, judgment and execution across organizational boundaries. Salesforce's digital-maturity expectations and joint innovation arrangements illustrate this direction. His questions about buying hours, documents, judgment or outcomes do not amount to an explicit prediction that hourly billing will disappear.

pts.k: Niles argues that trusted human–agent teams, explicit governance and the combination of senior expertise with curiosity are central to AI-enabled legal work.
pts.d: Niles identifies cross-functional human–AI collaboration as the next frontier for firms and legal departments. He argues that agents need defined roles, data access, permissions and enforceable prohibitions, and that enterprise governance practices should extend to firm–client relationships. He also claims senior lawyers' accumulated judgment and professional norms remain valuable: progress comes from applying that expertise to AI with curiosity, rather than discarding it. These are conditional and prescriptive claims, not measured findings about training or team performance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Niles's first-hand executive account of Salesforce deployments and professional experience, without quantitative evaluation.
pts.d: Niles grounds his claims in his role as Salesforce president and CLO, internal use of Salesforce technology, examples involving Slackbot and the outside counsel support agent, and collaboration through LCAio. His broader expectations draw on conversations with business leaders, in-house lawyers and law firms and his prior experience at Wachtell Lipton. The interview supplies no numerical productivity results, risk measurements, controlled comparisons, benchmarks or independent validation. The broader operating-model and teaming predictions are his interpretation and prescription. Salesforce's role as both software builder and internal user is explicitly acknowledged.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The July 2026 interview distinguishes current Salesforce deployments from an undated trajectory toward agents at scale and broader autonomous execution.
pts.d: The conversation follows Niles's March 2026 open letter. Internal agent use and partner digital-maturity expectations are described in the present tense; assignment and execution, autonomous processes and the shared operating system are presented as emerging directions without completion dates. Niles conditions successful adoption on trusted technology and data, clear agent permissions and restrictions, governance, human oversight and investment in staff AI fluency. He acknowledges Salesforce's advantages as an enterprise AI vendor able to deploy its own products, rather than establishing that all firms can immediately replicate its position.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal, compliance and risk teams, internal business clients, outside counsel and other professional-service partners.
pts.d: For Salesforce's legal teams, Niles anticipates less routine handling and greater focus on complex judgment, alongside responsibility for work allocation, governance and agent capabilities. Internal business clients receive faster, more self-service assistance. Outside firms and providers face expectations of comparable digital maturity and closer integration and co-development with the client. Legal operations and innovation teams work together through LCAio. Senior lawyers retain a role based on expertise, judgment and professional norms. The discussion concerns enterprise legal services; it makes no specific prediction about headcount, junior hiring, staffing leverage or access to justice.
